newsitem.title: USA: California governor proposes tort reforms.
newsitem.headline: California governor proposes tort reforms.

text.p: California Gov. Pete Wilson unveiled five tort reform measures Thursday, saying the changes are needed to maintain the state's economy and protect hundreds of thousands of jobs.

The governor said his proposals would help reduce arbitrary and unpredictable awards by providing standards to juries and judges, make it easier to dismiss meritless suits and defenses, and reduce the cost of litigation.
"Legal reform is one of the simplest, most sensible steps we can take this year to maintain the state's economic vigor," Wilson, a Republican, said in a statement.
"It is the loudest message this legislature can send that Sacramento is dead-serious about making California more attractive for jobs and investment," Wilson said.
The governor's proposal to reform punitive damages would establish standards for calculating punitive awards. These standards would provide more predictability, Wilson said.

The governor's wrongful termination reform proposal would reduce speculative future lost pay awards. Under this measure, Wilson said future lost pay may not exceed the amount of wages and benefits that the employee might reasonably earn for a five-year period following termination.
Wilson also proposed to reform certain types of lawsuits by shareholders.

Before bringing suit in the name of a corporation, Wilson said his measure would require the shareholder to either make a demand on the corporation's directors or allege facts specific to each director which show that the majority of directors could not fairly evaluate the shareholder's demand.

Wilson would also reform cases involving the unfair competition act, which allows anyone to sue against a business practice on behalf of the general public even if they have never suffered any harm or even been exposed to the practice.

Wilson said his proposal would require that attorneys bringing these suits have a real client who has been harmed or threatened with harm by the acts or practices prohibited under California's unfair competition act.

In addition, Wilson's proposals would conform California's summary judgement law to the standard used in the federal courts. Under this standard, summary judgement must be granted "unless there is sufficient evidence favoring the (opposing) party for a jury to return a verdict for that party."
